title: On the Difficulty of Learning a Meta-network for Training Data Selection
claim: The selection network's gradient signal-to-noise ratio is about an order of magnitude below the classifier's, but larger batches raise it.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend below, log-scale y-axis
description: Two side-by-side log-scale line plots titled 'PACS Photo→Art' and 'Texture'. The x-axis is batch size (64, 128, 256, 512, 1024) and the y-axis is GSNR. Each panel has four lines. Blue is the early training stage and orange is the middle training stage. Solid lines with circle markers are the selection network. Dashed lines with square markers are the classification network. All lines rise with batch size. The dashed classification curves sit roughly an order of magnitude above the solid selection curves. The middle-stage selection network (solid orange) is lowest, at about 1e-2 to 1e-1. The classification network at the early stage reaches about 6 on PACS and about 10 on Texture at batch size 1024. Light gray dashed gridlines are drawn. A single legend runs along the bottom. The eye goes first to the steep dashed blue line at the top and the gap between the dashed and solid lines.
caption: The gradient signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR) of the selection network is lower than that of the ResNet classification network by roughly one order of magnitude. However, increasing the batch size can help. Early and middle training stages correspond to 20% and 60% of the total training steps. Results are computed as averages over 100 batches.
abstract: Synthetic data are increasingly used to train neural networks, yet distributional mismatch with real data limits their effectiveness when used indiscriminately. A common strategy is to learn data weights via bi-level optimization, which we refer to as Meta-learning for Training-data Selection (MTS). Interestingly, in practice, MTS often performs below expectation. We identify two obstacles in properly training MTS: a poor gradient signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR), which causes optimization difficulties, and lack of informative features that correlates with data quality. We present a mathematical analysis of MTS, which reveals the dynamics of normalized data weights and the relation between disparate data quality and poor GSNR. The analysis suggests a a simple yet effective solution: increasing the batch size. Further, we propose a set of informative features that capture the positions of training data in their distributions and training dynamics. Experiments across four benchmarks show consistent improvements, achieving average gains of 5.49% over training without selection and 2.89% over the strongest baseline.
